from.title: The Cambridge History of Western Music Theory

topics.title: Tuning, temperament and consonance in history

attachTo.note: Extends the tools tuning-lab, overtone-player and consonance-ladder.

rules.text: Consonances are the ratios of the tetractys: 2:1 octave, 3:2 fifth, 4:3 fourth (plus 3:1 and 4:1).
rules.who: Pythagorean tradition (Division of the Canon; Nicomachus)

rules.text: The tone is the difference between fifth and fourth (9:8) and cannot be divided into two equal rational halves.
The ear, not number, judges intervals; a tetrachord spans a fourth of 2½ tones and is divided by two movable notes.
In the Pythagorean diatonic division every tone is 9:8 and every semitone within the tetrachord 256:243.
rules.who: Magadis in utraque parte (by c. 1100); Guido

rules.text: Pure thirds require a just division: major third 5:4, minor third 6:5.
In ¼-comma meantone each fifth is narrowed by ¼ of the syntonic comma so that four fifths give a pure major third.
In equal temperament each semitone is the twelfth root of 2 (100 cents).
Dissonance is roughness produced by beats between the partials of two tones.
Consonance is the degree to which two tones fuse into one impression.

terms.def: Four notes spanning a fourth; outer notes fixed, inner two movable by genus.
Enharmonic, chromatic or diatonic tuning of the tetrachord's inner notes.
Two-octave scale of four tetrachords plus proslambanomenos; mese is the centre.
Tonos: a transposition level of the system. Harmonia: an older scale-type with ethical character (Dorian, Phrygian…).
The Pythagorean minor (256:243) and major (2187:2048) semitones.
One-string instrument with a movable bridge for measuring intervals.
Tuning built from pure fifths (3:2) and octaves only.
Tuning with pure fifths and pure thirds (5:4, 6:5).
Pythagorean major third of two 9:8 tones (81:64), 22 cents sharper than 5:4.
81:80, about 21.5 cents: the difference between the Pythagorean and the just major third.
About 23.5 cents: twelve pure fifths minus seven octaves.
The one badly out-of-tune fifth that collects the error of a temperament.
1/1200 of an octave (Ellis).
Partials at whole-number multiples of a fundamental frequency.
Rameau's sounding body, whose partials generate the major triad.
Stumpf's measure of how far two tones are heard as one.
A third sound heard at the frequency difference of two loud tones (Tartini).

quiz.q: What is the Pythagorean ratio of the tone?
quiz.why: The difference between the fifth (3:2) and the fourth (4:3).

quiz.q: Why were thirds treated as imperfect or dissonant in Pythagorean tuning?
options: The ditone 81:64 is wider than the pure 5:4
They were not in the gamut
quiz.why: The ditone is about 22 cents wide.

quiz.q: What does ¼-comma meantone make pure?
quiz.why: Four narrowed fifths give a 5:4 third.

quiz.q: The difference between a Pythagorean and a just major third is the…

attachTo.note: Background to keys, scales and modes.

rules.text: Every key has either a major or a minor third above its final; the third decides the mode.

topics.title: Rameau: roots, inversion and the fundamental bass

attachTo.note: Background to chords and their inversions (ch4, ch7).

rules.text: Every chord has a fundamental (root); its inversions keep the same fundamental.
The fundamental bass should move by consonant intervals, chiefly fifths and thirds.
A dissonant seventh must resolve down by step.

guidelines.text: A chord such as F–A–C–D may be heard as IV with added sixth (going to I) or as ii7 (going to V): double emploi.

terms.def: The succession of chord roots underlying the actual bass.
Inversion: the same chord with another chord member in the bass.
Added sixth, characterizing the subdominant.
Double use: one chord with two possible fundamentals.
A note "supposed" below the fundamental, explaining ninth and eleventh chords.

quiz.q: Rameau's fundamental bass ideally moves by…

options: one chord read with two fundamentals

attachTo.note: Where Roman numerals (Weber) and function labels (Riemann) come from.

rules.text: Chords are named by the scale degree of their root (I–VII); upper case for major, lower case for minor.
Every root progression is ultimately by fifth or third; an apparent step implies a hidden intermediate root.
The minor triad is the inversion of the major: generated downward from its "root" (the fifth in ordinary terms).

guidelines.text: Function labels need not map neatly onto dualist chord roots; critics who reject Riemann on this ground overstate the case.

terms.def: Multiple meaning: a chord or pitch interpretable in several keys.
Scale degree; also a harmonic span governed by one degree (Schenker).
"Hybrid chord" (Sechter/Mayrberger), mixing elements of two keys.
The view that major and minor are generated in opposite directions and are equal in status.
Riemann's term for a triad as a unit with a principal tone.
Riemann's chord transformations: a move that keeps the mode / one that changes it.
Neo-Riemannian Parallel, Leading-tone exchange, Relative.

quiz.q: Sechter explains stepwise root motion by…
quiz.why: All roots move by fifths or thirds.

quiz.q: In Riemann's dualism the principal tone of a minor triad is…
quiz.why: The Unterklang hangs downward from it.

quiz.q: Which neo-Riemannian operation turns C major into A minor?
quiz.why: Relative: keep C and E, move G to A.

rules.text: The fundamental line descends stepwise to ① from ③, ⑤ or ⑧; the bass arpeggiates I–V–I beneath it.
A dissonant passing tone cannot itself be prolonged; only a consonance can be composed out.

terms.def: Fundamental structure: Urlinie plus Bassbrechung.
Fundamental line descending to the tonic.
Bass arpeggiation I–V–I.
Elaboration that keeps a structural event in force across a span.
Interruption: ③–② ‖ ③–②–①.

quiz.why: The first descent stops on ②.

tools.title: Monochord & tuning lab
tools.spec: Pick a system: Pythagorean (fifths E♭–G♯), just (C major, Ramis/Salinas type), ¼-comma meantone, 2/7-comma (Zarlino), ⅙-comma, Werckmeister III, equal. Show a 12-note table of cents relative to C, plus the size of every fifth and major third with its deviation from pure (colour scale; the wolf flagged). Play: scale, chosen triad, the wolf fifth. Playback detunes the harpsichord by fractional MIDI (cents/100). Second panel: Greek tetrachord genera in Aristoxenian parts (fourth = 30 parts): enharmonic 3+3+24, soft chromatic 4+4+22, hemiolic 4½+4½+21, tonic chromatic 6+6+18, soft diatonic 6+9+15, intense diatonic 6+12+12; play descending as the Greeks listed them.
tests: ¼-comma meantone: C–E = 386.3 c, every fifth 696.6 c, G♯–E♭ wolf ≈ 737.6 c
Pythagorean: C–E = 407.8 c; fifth G♯–E♭ ≈ 678.5 c
Equal: every interval a multiple of 100 c

tools.title: Rameau's fundamental bass
tools.spec: Input chords as pitch-letter groups separated by "|" (e.g., C E G | F A C D | G B D F | C E G). For each chord find the root by stacking thirds; for F–A–C–D show both readings (IV add6 / ii7, double emploi). Draw the actual bass and the fundamental bass on two staves; label each root move as 5th/4th (cadential), 3rd, or step (flag: Rameau/Sechter would explain with a hidden root). Play actual and fundamental bass.
tests: C–E–G → root C; E–G–C → root C (inversion)
G–B–D–F → root G, seventh F resolves down

tools.title: Tonnetz & Riemann transformations
tools.spec: A triangular lattice of pitch classes (fifths horizontal, major thirds diagonal). Triangles are triads. Buttons P, L, R (and chains like LR, PL) move the current triad; show its name, the dualist reading (Oberklang from root / Unterklang from fifth) and the path. Play each triad.
tests: Alternating P and L returns to C+ after 6 moves (hexatonic cycle)

tools.title: Ursatz viewer
tools.spec: Choose 3-, 5- or 8-line, major/minor, and interruption on/off. Show the Ursatz in two voices: Urlinie (open noteheads with ^ degree numbers and a beam) over Bassbrechung I–V–I. Play it; then optionally play a simple middleground (e.g., ③–②–① with a neighbour or an initial ascent).
